description: Born after 1945 to protect every citizen against illness, unemployment and old age, the welfare state is now shaken by aging populations and by globalization.

hero.hook: In 1960, France had four working people paying for each retiree. Today there are barely two.

blocks.text: The **welfare state** is the whole set of supports a government gives its citizens to protect them against illness, unemployment and old age. In its modern form the system was born just after the Second World War, as a promise of collective solidarity.

Since the end of the 20th century, this pillar of developed societies has been going through a funding crisis. Aging populations, globalization, new forms of work: the balance between social protection and the economy is being questioned everywhere in the world.

In 1942, the British economist William Beveridge published a report that would become a founding text: [[The Beveridge Report]]. His ambition was to protect every citizen against five great evils: disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness and want.

France followed the same path in 1945 by creating its social security system. It grew out of a political compromise reached inside the [[National Council of the Resistance]], the body that had united the resistance movements during the war. The state no longer limited itself to policing and justice. It became the guarantor of everyone's well-being.
The welfare state was not invented by socialists but by the conservative German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1883. His aim was strategic: to calm the workers and head off a revolution.

sections.title: 1945: the birth of a social contract

blocks.text: The postwar balance broke down under two big changes. The first is demographic: people live longer and families have fewer children. That raises health spending and lengthens the time each person draws a pension.

blocks.caption: An aging population weighs more heavily on the social accounts every year

blocks.text: In France, four working people paid for each retiree in the 1960s. Today the figure has fallen below two. The second change is the rise of unemployment since the oil shocks of 1973, together with the growth of the [[gig economy]], those independent and insecure jobs that pay less into the system while being more exposed to risk.

In a globalized economy, companies and capital move easily from one country to another. The taxes and contributions needed to fund social protection then look like a handicap next to countries where labor is cheaper.

The Nordic countries are an interesting counter-example. Sweden and Denmark keep a high level of social protection while staying very competitive. Their secret has a name: [[flexicurity]]. Firms can lay people off easily, but in exchange workers get generous unemployment benefits and strong support in finding a new job.
Denmark spends about 32% of its GDP on social protection, one of the highest rates in the world, and is still regularly ranked among the easiest countries in which to start a business.

sections.title: Globalization puts the model under pressure

blocks.text: Tomorrow's system has to cover new risks: the uberization of work, the green transition, and the loss of independence that comes with very old age. The French reform of 2023, which pushed the legal retirement age to 64, shows how hard these changes are to get accepted.

The debate is also about funding. Should the bulk of the system keep resting on wages, at the risk of penalizing employment, or should it shift toward broader funding through taxation, like the [[CSG]] in France, a levy that touches every kind of income and not only salaries?

The welfare state, born in 1945 to protect everyone against illness, unemployment and old age, has been weakened by unprecedented aging and by globalization. Its survival will depend on its ability to reinvent itself without losing its promise of solidarity.
